humanities_role_explanation: Evaluates LLM domain-specific competence in diplomatic transcription and period-specific orthographic preservation of 18th-century Russian Civil font, assessing errors like temporal conflation and over-historicization.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Combines scanned historical page or line images with textual prompts to evaluate multimodal LLMs on OCR/transcription tasks.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Involves visual character and layout recognition of historical Cyrillic Civil print and diplomatic transcription, including post-OCR error correction experiments.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Scoped specifically to historical document OCR and diplomatic transcription of 18th-century Russian Civil font.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluated 12 generative multimodal LLMs, including GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, Claude 3.5/3.7, Gemini 2.0/2.5, and Qwen2.5-VL.

quantitative_metrics.note: Uses standard metrics (CER, WER) alongside novel domain-specific metrics (Historical Character Preservation Rate, Archaic Insertion Rate, Case Error Rate).

summary: This paper presents a methodological framework for evaluating LLM-based historical document OCR, utilizing a newly digitized dataset of 18th-century Russian books printed in Civil font. The authors investigate how prompt engineering, processing modes, and document features affect model accuracy and stability. Additionally, they introduce novel metrics to expose 'over-historicization' biases, where models inappropriately insert pre-reform, medieval characters into texts.
key_findings: Gemini-2.5-Pro achieved the highest OCR accuracy and stability (3.36% CER and 4.69% WER in full-page mode). OpenAI models frequently exhibited 'over-historicization' errors, introducing pre-Petrine characters (e.g., little yus and omega) in up to 59% of files for GPT-4o. Post-OCR correction using LLMs degraded rather than improved the transcription quality.
facets_explanation: The reference ground truth was created through a multi-stage process where initial OCR generated by a fine-tuned TrOCR model was subjected to 100% manual correction and a two-pass protocol by a single expert annotator. The task is diplomatic transcription of 18th-century Russian page images and does not require external historical knowledge beyond the visual stimulus. Evaluation is performed by comparing the generated text to a single gold-standard reference using distance metrics like CER and WER. Divergences or disagreements between annotators are not explicitly discussed or preserved, though a verification audit showed high agreement.
